citations.quote: Applying Model-Based System Engineering (MBSE) tools to developing Cislunar missions has been proposed to decrease costs and increase reliability for future missions.

This Thesis assesses the maturity and applicability of the CSRM in the context of designing Cislunar CubeSat missions. This Thesis uses MBSE methodologies to determine the commonality and differences in space mission architectures and Mission Engineering tasks and components of LEO and Cislunar space missions.

The idea is that by starting with a standard architecture, a mission development team is able to save time and effort when creating their mission architecture using traditional systems engineering processes. Compared to having to start from scratch, it can be used for a relatively low cost, the CSRM is reusable (with changes in physical instantiation due to the relatively simple, standardized nature of cubesat interfaces and systems, and 'focused' mission goals), for the development of simulations and trade studies with built-in traceback and flow down capability.

The CSRM is based on Model-Based System Engineering (MBSE) principles, is System Modeling Language (SysML) compliant, is hosted in a graphical modeling tool, and is intended to foster completeness and economies of scale associated with reusability [4]. The MBSE-based CSRM is intended to be relatively easy to modify (compared to traditional documentation-based systems processes) with the goal of lowering the time and cost for implementing and tracking changes and their subsequent flow-down effects.

The OMG defines the CSRM as describing "the necessary stereotypes (extends SysML) for logical CubeSat space-ground architectures. The profile is intended to promote consistency and interoperability of logical CubeSat space/ground architecture models. The profile is intended to be used as-is or extended." [14].

Two previous SSWG studies, [16] and [17], assessed where the CSRM currently supports MEng activities and identified areas that require further research. It proposed a way forward that defined research activities to specify extensions to the CSRM needed to support the MEng of a CubeSat mission.

The SSWG created the CSRM as a starting point for system engineers to develop a physical architecture for their CubeSat mission. As a logical space-ground architecture, logical components are abstractions of the physical components that perform the system functionality without imposing implementation constraints.

The CSRM integrates five overarching elements: 1) Stakeholders, 2) Technical Measures, 3) Behaviors, 4) Requirements, and 5) Architecture. The CSRM provides for defining and tracing requirements from stakeholders to behaviors, with technical measures assigned to subsystems and components to be certified through validation and verification activities [12].

citations.quote: The point of the CSRM is to be a generalized MBSE model for CubeSat missions that is reusable across various mission types. These missions in Earth Orbit themselves can have large varieties and variations, including LEO, high eccentricity orbits or geostationary orbit missions. Eventually, the CSRM would want to be accessible to other interplanetary targets beyond Earth’s Moon.

Adding specific elements for a lunar mission would require additional model development, validation, and verification resources. It may also necessitate specialized knowledge and expertise in lunar mission design, which may not be readily available within the INCOSE team developing the CSRM.

The onboarding ramp for implementing a physical model for an actual mission using the CSRM could be estimated to be <120 work hours for an experienced Systems Engineer and <360 hours for an inexperienced engineer.

The three missions used were the Arizona State University (ASU) Phoenix CubeSat, Morehead State University (MSU)’s Lunar IceCube Mission and NASA's CAPSTONE.

MSU's Lunar IceCube was a university-built 6U cubesat primarily built from COTS components, many of which were used for the first time beyond LEO, but with a NASA GSFC payload and JPL science principal investigator.

Constraints may include limited communication bandwidth, orbital debris avoidance, and power limitations based on solar exposure. Lunar orbit mission requirements are nearly identical, except they are Moon-centric. Some extend to factors like lunar lighting conditions, communication delays due to the increased distance from Earth, and fuel requirements for complex maneuvers.

Performance measures and methods for both LEO and Lunar orbit missions utilize similar metrics like data collection rates, navigation accuracy, communication reliability, power consumption, and payload functionality. Methods for both involve telemetry monitoring, ground testing, and simulations.

For this analysis, 200 CSRM elements were "mapped" or sorted under its "singular" and "closest" MEng Artifact (in Appendix B) or SMA Element (in Appendix C). Determinations were categorized as Fully (100%), Mostly (>50%), Partially (<50%), or Not Captured (0%) based on how many and the quality of the CSRM elements represented in the MEng artifacts and SMA elements.
